name: Monochrome and vertical-line outfits

lead: Wearing one colour, or vertical lines, from head to toe creates an unbroken visual line that style communities say makes the wearer look taller and longer. The effect is visual and shows straight away.

An unbroken colour or line leads the eye vertically and avoids cutting the body into segments. Proponents cite the vertical-horizontal illusion, in which vertical lines tend to be overestimated relative to equal horizontal lines; that research concerns line drawings, not clothing, and no clothing-specific studies were found.

paras: People build outfits in a single colour family, often dark tones, or choose pinstripes and other vertical patterns, and match shoe and trouser colour to avoid a break at the ankle.
Low risk. Fit and colour choice affect how the outfit looks on different builds.

angle.text: Monochrome outfits and vertical lines create an unbroken line that makes the wearer look taller and longer. The effect is visual and immediate; the supporting illusion research concerns lines rather than clothing.

lead: Monochrome and vertical-line outfits are a styling approach in which clothing in a single colour, or with vertical stripes and seams, is worn from top to shoes so that the body reads as one unbroken line. People use it to look taller and leaner, because a continuous colour avoids visual breaks at the waist and a vertical pattern draws the eye up and down rather than across.

Proponents often cite the vertical-horizontal illusion, in which a vertical line tends to be overestimated relative to an equal horizontal line; the effect persists even when viewers know the lines are the same length, and it is largest in L-shaped and inverted-T line figures [1]. That research concerns line drawings, and the Wikipedia article on it does not address clothing [1].

Style advice from the T Nation forum shows the same ideas circulating in practice: in one thread about dressing a short woman, a poster mentions cropped ankle-length trousers as a trick for shorter people [2]. No study of colour-blocking or striped clothing and perceived height was found.
infobox: Unbroken visual line, apparent height and slimness
Tonal outfits, vertical stripes, seams, cropped ankle trousers

paras: Proponents say wearing similar tones from top to shoes avoids visual breaks at the waist, and that vertical stripes or seams draw the eye up and down. Matching the shoe colour to the trouser colour is a common way to extend the leg line, and a monochrome outfit is often described as easy to assemble.

The vertical-horizontal illusion is the tendency to overestimate a vertical line relative to an equal horizontal one, and it persists even when people know the lines are equal [1]. The illusion is strongest in L, plus and inverted-T arrangements, and it decreases between ages eight and fourteen according to a 1907 study of schoolchildren cited by Wikipedia [1]. Urban populations are reported as more susceptible than rural ones, though the differences are described as inconsistent [1]. The article does not discuss clothing.

Posts on T Nation reference tricks like cropped ankle-length pants for shorter people, in a thread where a poster suggests outfit ideas to a woman who is about 5 feet 2 inches tall [2]. Dedicated discussion of monochrome or vertical-line dressing was not found beyond such mentions.
No studies found on clothing colour or stripes and perceived height.
